strengths: Addresses several real, underexplored limitations in video-to-audio generation simultaneously: long-form generation, few-step sampling, and audio conditioning/outpainting, rather than optimizing a single axis.

Synchronization—the paper's central claim—is supported by two complementary signals: the DeSync objective metric (0.497 vs MMAudio's 0.521) and the human listening study (Sync MOS 3.52 vs 2.92), which is the paper's most convincing evidence.

The shortcut ablation (Table 2) is a meaningful and well-designed control: it shows the shortcut objective incurs essentially no fidelity loss relative to vanilla flow matching at full sampling steps, which is the key claim needed to justify the approach over reflow-style distillation.

The few-step and duration sweeps (Figure 5) are informative and show a clear, robust advantage of SALSA-V over MMAudio in low-step and long-duration regimes, with SALSA-V degrading much more gracefully.

The custom contrastive synchronization model built on a larger pretrained backbone (VideoPrism) with a reasoned argument about batch size and hard negatives is a sensible, well-motivated design choice.
The appendix is thorough, providing implementation details, the masked-inference formulation, and the SWSD algorithm, which aids reproducibility of the method itself.
Qualitative spectrogram evidence (Figures 3, 4, 8, 9) is well-chosen and illustrates the intended behaviors (event alignment, outpainting, conditioning without over-reliance on ground truth).
An honest limitations section acknowledges the subjective quality gap to MMAudio and the failure mode of progressive outpainting across scene cuts.
weaknesses: The main quantitative comparison (Table 1) includes only two baselines, one of which (FoleyCrafter, 2024) is comparatively dated. Notably absent are Frieren (the rectified-flow/reflow model that is the natural baseline for the few-step claim), V-AURA (the autoregressive long-form baseline), LoVA (dedicated long-form work), and Diff-Foley—all discussed in related work but never compared against. This omission directly undermines the 'few-step' and 'long-form' contribution claims.

Most objective metrics show only marginal differences from MMAudio, and some favor the baseline (KL_PANN+ 1.81 vs 1.77; IS 17.85 vs 18.13). The claim of 'significantly outperforms' rests almost entirely on synchronization, so the breadth of the contribution is narrower than the framing suggests.

The human study is small (18 participants, 10 trials, 180 total scores, ~60 per method) and reports no confidence intervals or significance tests, making the overall-quality and fidelity conclusions (3.43 vs 3.29) statistically weak. Given that these deltas are within plausible noise, the strong subjective claims are not fully supported.

The long-form comparison is not apples-to-apples and the authors acknowledge this: MMAudio processes the full sequence at once while SALSA-V uses progressive outpainting with a 0.5 s reference, which the authors concede may advantage MMAudio below ~20 s. The resulting comparison therefore does not cleanly isolate the claimed long-form capability.

SWSD is a self-defined metric with no external validation, and the audio-conditioning claim (Section A.2) is supported primarily by this new metric on a hand-selected 'representative subset' of clips that contain characteristic sounds. The spectral-fidelity claim thus rests on a metric and subset chosen by the authors.

The ablation study (Table 2) only varies model size and the shortcut/flow-matching objective. The two other central components—the masked training objective and the custom synchronization backbone—are not ablated, so their individual contributions are not isolated (e.g., no comparison against Synchformer-based conditioning).

Reproducibility is limited: no code or checkpoint release is mentioned, training uses a proprietary 'high-fidelity studio Foley set' that is neither described nor released, and training is done on TPU v4-8 in JAX/Flax. The filtering pipeline (using the model's own sync model to select training data) is also self-referential and hard to replicate.

Novelty is largely integrative: shortcut models (Frans et al., 2025), masked flow matching (Chen et al., 2025), contrastive AV synchronization (Synchformer lineage), and MMDiT/DiT blocks are all prior art. The contribution is the first application of these to V2A rather than new methodology, which limits originality.

Ethical considerations are not discussed at all—no mention of consent/licensing for the in-the-wild YouTube/Panda70M data, nor of the potential for misuse (generating plausible Foley audio for arbitrary real videos).

strengths: Addresses an important and timely set of problems in video-to-audio generation: precise synchronization, long-form generation, few-step sampling, and audio-conditioned generation.

Integrates shortcut models into a V2A/audio flow-matching pipeline, and the ablation at 32 sampling steps suggests no fidelity loss relative to vanilla flow matching (Table 2), which is a practically useful direction.

Uses a larger pretrained VideoPrism backbone plus AST with a SigLIP contrastive objective for synchronization features; the human study reports improved perceived synchronization (3.52 vs. 2.92 for MMAudio).
The masked flow-matching objective enables audio in/outpainting and iterative long-form extension; qualitative examples and SWSD/FAD curves suggest conditioning transfers spectral characteristics.
Reports both objective and human evaluation, includes an honest limitations section, and provides implementation details such as VAE fine-tuning and training hyperparameters.
weaknesses: The central claim that SALSA-V 'significantly outperforms' state of the art is not supported by the evidence: FAD_VGG is 1.07 vs. 1.12, DeSync is 0.497 vs. 0.521 (below the 0.2 s resolution of the metric), and IB is 33.76 vs. 32.89, while KL_PANNs (1.81 vs. 1.77), IS (17.85 vs. 18.13), and human audio quality (2.96 vs. 3.16) are worse than MMAudio. No statistical significance tests, confidence intervals, or repeated-sampling error bars are reported.

The long-form comparison is not apples-to-apples: SALSA-V uses iterative 10 s chunk outpainting with a 0.5 s reference, whereas MMAudio processes the full sequence at once. The paper itself notes MMAudio has full context until roughly 20 s, making the comparison confounded. There is no long-form human evaluation, no semantic-consistency metric, and no analysis of drift or error accumulation over many extensions.
The baseline set is incomplete: no comparison with Frieren, V-AURA, LoVA, or other recent long-form/few-step V2A methods, despite these being directly relevant to the claimed contributions.

Novelty is incremental: the masked flow-matching objective closely follows Chen et al. (2025), the shortcut loss is adopted from Frans et al. (2025), and the contrastive synchronization features follow Synchformer/MMAudio-style designs. The paper does not isolate whether VideoPrism-based synchronization features actually outperform Synchformer features or are necessary for the reported gains.

Key components are not ablated: there is no ablation of the masked objective versus standard flow matching, no comparison of shortcut versus vanilla flow matching at 1/2/4/8 sampling steps (Table 2 is only at 32 steps), no ablation of the fine-tuned 43 Hz VAE, and no text-conditioning ablation.

The 'unconstrained length' claim is overclaimed. The model still has a finite context window and relies on progressive outpainting, which can drift and accumulate errors; the limitations section admits failures at scene cuts, but no experiments beyond 60 s or on multi-scene content are provided.
The 'near-real-time' claim is not measured. There are no runtime, latency, throughput, FLOPs, or hardware comparisons at 8 sampling steps, so practical usability remains unsupported.

The 'professional audio synthesis/Foley' claim is weakly supported: there is no audio-conditioning baseline, no human evaluation for sound design, and the proposed SWSD metric is self-defined, unvalidated, and not compared against alternatives.

The human study is underpowered and underdocumented: 18 'qualified' participants, 10 videos, and 180 scores, with no statistical analysis, no recruitment or qualification details, no IRB/consent/compensation discussion, and no inter-rater reliability. The web interface also raises timing-drift concerns that are mentioned but not quantified.

Reproducibility is limited: no code or checkpoints are released, the sample URL is blank in the manuscript, filtering thresholds for YouTube/Panda70M data are unspecified, and important training/evaluation details (architecture specifics, compute budget, data splits, test-set composition) are incomplete.

Metric reliability is questionable: FAD_VGG, KL, and IS on an unspecified or small test set can be unstable, and no confidence intervals or repeated evaluations are reported. The DeSync difference of 0.024 s is far below the stated 0.2 s resolution.

Presentation and clarity issues remain: the typo 'KLPANN+' appears in the main table, table columns and metric definitions are ambiguous, several method details are relegated to the appendix, and the abstract/introduction overclaim relative to the evidence.

Research ethics are not adequately addressed: there is no discussion of licensing, privacy, or consent for in-the-wild YouTube/Panda70M data, nor of ethical review for the human listening study, despite the paper's use of human subjects and copyrighted media.

The limitations discussion is honest about subjective audio quality and scene-cut failures, but it does not engage with the more serious issues of statistical significance, confounded long-form evaluation, missing baselines, or reproducibility.

strengths: Targets genuinely under-addressed problems in V2A generation: long-form synthesis, few-step sampling, and audio conditioning/controllability, which most prior work (MMAudio, Frieren) leaves open.

Introduces the first application of shortcut models to video-to-audio (and general audio), enabling 8-step sampling without a separate distillation/refinement stage; Table 2 shows the shortcut objective does not degrade fidelity at 32 steps relative to vanilla flow matching.

Replaces the commonly used Synchformer features with a VideoPrism-based contrastive synchronization model, with a well-motivated analysis of batch size and hard negatives (Section 3.1) that is consistent with prior findings.
Strong and internally consistent synchronization results: best DeSync (0.497) and a clear human-rated synchronization lead over MMAudio (3.52 vs 2.92), achieved with a smaller model (643M vs 1.03B).

Comprehensive evaluation package: multiple distribution-matching/quality metrics, a blind randomized human listening study (Section A.3), qualitative spectrogram case studies (Figures 3, 4, 8, 9), and ablations over model size and training objective (Table 2).

Clear presentation with informative figures, a detailed appendix (implementation, VAE fine-tuning, inference masking, a novel SWSD metric with an algorithm listing), and an honest, specific limitations section.
weaknesses: The central few-step claim is not directly ablated: the shortcut-vs-flow-matching comparison in Table 2 is only at 32 steps, and no experiment shows the vanilla FM model degrading at low step counts. Thus the causal attribution of few-step capability to the shortcut loss is not established, and the low-step curve in Figure 5 is only against MMAudio.

Frieren, the most directly relevant efficient V2A baseline (rectified flow + reflow distillation), is discussed in Related Work but never compared, despite being the natural competitor for the sampling-efficiency contribution.

The abstract/intro claim that SALSA-V 'significantly outperforms' SOTA is overstated: IS (17.85 vs 18.13), IB (33.76 vs 32.89), and KL_PANNs (1.81 vs 1.77) are essentially tied or slightly worse, and human audio quality is lower than MMAudio (2.96 vs 3.16). The only decisive wins are DeSync and human synchronization.

Audio-conditioning and long-form results are largely qualitative or self-referential. Long-form is only compared to MMAudio via FAD/DeSync, with no external baselines for audio-conditioned generation, and the 'dedicated set of single-shot, long-form testing data' is not described in enough detail to reproduce.

Reproducibility is partial: no code/weights release is indicated (samples only), some training data is private or non-public (high-fidelity studio Foley set, filtered in-the-wild YouTube/Panda70M), and training is done on TPU v4-8, limiting independent reproduction.

The human study is modest in scale (18 participants, 10 trials each, 180 scores) and no significance testing or inter-rater analysis is reported, so the small human-rating gaps (e.g., overall 3.43 vs 3.29) are hard to interpret as reliable.

strengths: Strong and well-supported synchronization contribution: SALSA-V achieves the best DeSync (0.497 vs. MMAudio's 0.521) and a notably higher human synchronization MOS (3.52 vs. 2.92), which is the paper's most convincing result and is backed by both quantitative metrics and a human listening study.

The application of the shortcut/self-consistency loss to video-to-audio is a genuinely novel and well-motivated contribution. Table 2 shows it incurs essentially no fidelity loss versus vanilla flow matching at 32 steps, and Figure 4/Table 3 demonstrate that quality and synchronization degrade far more gracefully than MMAudio/Frieren in the few-step regime, enabling near-real-time generation without a separate distillation stage.

Comprehensive multi-axis evaluation: distribution-matching metrics (FAD/KL), reference-free quality (IS), semantic alignment (IB), temporal synchronization (DeSync), human MOS, few-step scaling, long-form scaling, and generation latency. The combination gives a reasonably complete picture of the model's behavior.

The long-form evaluation (Figure 4, Table 5 vs. LoVA at 30s) addresses a real gap in prior V2A work, and the masked-training objective is a sensible mechanism to support both audio conditioning/outpainting and chunked extension, with the conditioning behavior quantified via FAD and the proposed SWSD metric (Figure 6).

Honest and appropriate treatment of limitations (scene-cut failure of progressive outpainting) and research ethics (media-manipulation risks in the impact statement), plus detailed training/hyperparameter reporting in the appendix.
weaknesses: The abstract and introduction claim 'unconstrained length' / 'seamless synthesis of unconstrained length audio sequences,' but the actual mechanism is chunked extension conditioned on a fixed ~10s context via progressive outpainting. This is not truly unconstrained generation, and the authors themselves note it breaks down across scene cuts. The framing overstates the contribution relative to what is demonstrated.

The contrastively-trained synchronization model is a headline contribution, yet there is no controlled ablation isolating it: the paper hypothesizes that the VideoPrism backbone alleviates missed-event failure modes but never compares its sync features against the Synchformer-based conditioning used by MMAudio. The claim that the new backbone improves synchronization is therefore not directly verified.

The human study is small (18 participants, 180 scores) and compares only against MMAudio and FoleyCrafter, not the full set of baselines. Differences in overall quality (3.43 vs. 3.29) are small and no significance testing is reported anywhere, despite several objective gaps being marginal (e.g., FAD 1.07 vs. 1.12, IB 33.76 vs. 32.89).

The masked in/outpainting objective is adapted from prior work (VampNet, Chen et al. 2025), so the novelty there is largely incremental; the paper does not clearly disentangle how much of the conditioning/outpainting ability is due to the masking scheme versus the model/architecture.

Reproducibility is limited: no code or model release is mentioned, training uses private data (a studio Foley set, filtered in-the-wild YouTube from Panda70M) and TPU v4-8 hardware, and the fine-tuned 43 Hz VAE is only briefly described. The headline few-step claim also rests on a single shortcut-vs-flow-matching comparison at 32 steps, with the more interesting intermediate-step behavior shown only against MMAudio rather than against the authors' own converged 32-step model in tabular form.

strengths: Addresses several important video-to-audio challenges in one framework: precise synchronization, long-form generation, audio conditioning, and few-step sampling.

Integrates shortcut models into video-to-audio generation and provides promising empirical evidence for few-step sampling without post-hoc distillation (Figure 4, Table 3), while showing no degradation at 32 steps in Table 2.
Long-form generation via masked flow matching and iterative outpainting achieves strong objective results against LoVA on 30-second samples (Table 5) and maintains FAD/DeSync across longer durations.
Uses a larger pretrained VideoPrism backbone for synchronization features and reports improved human-rated synchronization over MMAudio (3.52 vs. 2.92).
Includes a human listening study, detailed implementation appendix, qualitative spectrogram analyses, and an impact statement.
weaknesses: The shortcut self-consistency target appears technically incorrect: the second velocity term is evaluated at time t rather than t+d, which is inconsistent with the stated derivation and undermines a central few-step generation claim.
There is no ablation of the proposed contrastive synchronization model against Synchformer or the synchronization features used by MMAudio, so the source of the synchronization gains is not isolated.

The masked flow-matching objective is not ablated; audio conditioning and long-form claims rely on qualitative examples and self-comparisons rather than baselines or rigorous inpainting/outpainting metrics.

Evaluation may be unfair: Table 1 uses variable-length videos up to 30 seconds, which disadvantages baselines trained with 10-second positional embeddings; fixed-length comparisons are missing. The human study also uses variable-length videos, potentially biasing results.

The human evaluation is underpowered and inconsistently reported: 18 participants and 10 videos, ambiguous "180 individual scores" despite 3 tracks and 3 aspects per trial, no significance tests, no inter-annotator agreement, and no clear participant qualification details. Strong baselines such as AudioX and LoVA are excluded from the human study.

Claims of significantly outperforming state of the art are overstated: human-rated audio quality is lower than MMAudio (2.96 vs. 3.16), and several objective gains are small (e.g., FAD 1.07 vs. 1.12, DeSync 0.497 vs. 0.521) without statistical testing.

The "unconstrained length" claim is overstated: long-form generation uses iterative extension with only a 0.5-second reference, lacks global consistency/seam metrics, and has no long-form human evaluation; drift and scene-change issues are acknowledged but not quantified.
Audio conditioning is evaluated with a non-standard "per-sample FAD" (Fréchet distance requires distributions) and an unvalidated SWSD metric, without comparison to conditioning baselines.

Reproducibility is limited: no code or models are released, the Foley data is proprietary, training data is filtered using the authors' own synchronization model, and text supervision for in-the-wild video data is unclear.

Presentation and ethics issues remain: reference formatting errors, ambiguous human-evaluation axes ("Overall" vs. "Overall Fit"), no IRB/consent details for the listening study, and no licensing/consent discussion for YouTube/Panda70M data.

strengths: The paper makes a meaningful and timely contribution to video-to-audio generation by combining masked flow matching, shortcut-based few-step sampling, and a new contrastive synchronization feature extractor. The combination addresses controllability, long-form generation, and inference speed in a single model.

The empirical results are strong on the most relevant axes: SALSA-V achieves the best DeSync (0.497 vs. MMAudio 0.521), best ImageBind (33.76), and best FAD_VGG (1.07) in Table 1, and leads the human study in Overall (3.43) and Synchronization (3.52). The long-form comparison against LoVA (Table 5) and few-step comparison against Frieren reflow (Table 3) further support the main claims.

The shortcut formulation is adopted for the first time in video-to-audio/general audio generation. Table 2 shows that the shortcut objective does not degrade full-step (32-step) quality relative to an identical flow-matching model, and Table 4 shows practical efficiency (0.71s for 10s audio at 4 steps).

The masked training objective enables both audio-conditioned generation and iterative outpainting. Qualitative examples (Figures 5 and 9) and quantitative SWSD/FAD analysis in Appendix A.3 provide useful evidence that the model can transfer spectral characteristics from a reference audio segment.

The paper includes a blind, randomized human listening study with MOS ratings along overall fit, synchronization, and audio quality, which is valuable for evaluating perceptual synchronization beyond objective metrics.

Implementation details are extensive (architecture, training schedules, optimizer, batch sizes, VAE fine-tuning, data filtering, inference masking, human interface), which aids reproducibility compared to many V2A papers.
The impact statement appropriately acknowledges misuse risks around media manipulation and suggests safeguards.
weaknesses: The contribution of the proposed synchronization feature model is not isolated. The paper hypothesizes that Synchformer features suffer from limited pretraining data and that a VideoPrism-based contrastive model fixes this, but there is no ablation replacing the synchronization features with Synchformer/MMAudio-style features or comparing synchronization-model accuracy directly. Thus the SOTA synchronization result cannot be confidently attributed to the new contrastive model.

The masked training objective is central to the audio-conditioning and long-form claims, but there is no ablation against a no-mask model for either conditioning fidelity or long-form outpainting. The comparison to MMAudio/LoVA shows the full system is better, but it does not establish that masking is the causal factor.

The shortcut loss is not directly ablated at low sampling steps. Table 2 only compares shortcut vs. flow matching at 32 steps; the few-step claim would be stronger with a flow-matching version of SALSA-V evaluated at 4/8 steps. The Frieren reflow comparison (Table 3) is useful but does not isolate the shortcut objective.

The human evaluation has limitations: only 18 participants and 10 videos, no confidence intervals or significance tests, and an apparent inconsistency in the number of scores (the design implies 18 participants x 10 videos x 3 aspects = 540 ratings if only one track per video, or 1620 if three tracks per video; the reported 180 is inconsistent). Human quality is also lower than MMAudio (2.96 vs. 3.16), which weakens the broad 'outperforms' framing. The human study also omits AudioX, which is strongest on some objective metrics, so the perceptual comparison is not against the full current SOTA.

Long-form evaluation fairness is debatable. MMAudio is trained/evaluated on 10s clips; evaluating it on 30-60s full sequences may be out-of-distribution, as the paper acknowledges. The proposed 'unconstrained length' claim is really iterative 10s-context outpainting, and the limitations section notes scene-cut and drift issues. A fairer long-form baseline would use MMAudio with chunked inference or retraining.

Reproducibility is only partial. No code or checkpoints are released; training uses non-public in-the-wild YouTube/Panda70M data and a proprietary high-fidelity studio Foley set; the evaluation test set includes holdout in-the-wild videos. The VAE fine-tuning and data filtering also depend on the authors' internal synchronization model, making exact reproduction difficult.

Objective quality metrics are mixed: SALSA-V is not best on IS (17.85 vs. AudioX 18.05 and MMAudio 18.13) or KL_PANNs (1.81 vs. AudioX 1.70), and the abstract/claim of 'significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in both audiovisual alignment and synchronization' overstates the alignment/quality picture. The contribution is strongest for synchronization and long-form, not for all metrics.

Some methodological details are underspecified or inconsistent: the main text says masks span 5 ms to 2.5 s, while Appendix A.5 says 1 to 88 latent tokens (roughly 0.023-2.05 s at 43 Hz); the self-consistency loss description omits details of the d sampling distribution and loss weighting. These are minor but affect reproducibility.
